                CARPENTER LAND AND CATTLE CO.’S INITIAL BRIEF

       Carpenter Land and Cattle Co. (Carpenter) files this Initial Brief and urges that if the

Honorable Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) and the Public Utility Commission of Texas

(Commission) are inclined to determine that the Applicants have introduced evidence to

sufficiently prove the public necessity for the proposed project, that it only approve the project if

it can do so by approving a route for the proposed line that does not materially damage the use and

enjoyment of the Texas State Parks on the Colorado River.             Pursuant to State Office of

Administrative Hearings (SOAH) Order No. 32 Addressing Post-Hearing Matters, this Initial Brief

is timely filed on or before June 19, 2026.


                                     I. INTRODUCTION

       In the interest of judicial efficiency in avoiding repetition and out of respect for the ALJs’

time, much of the discussion of the evidence that supports the selection of Route 296 is contained

in the Initial Brief of Save the Lampasas and is incorporated by reference here. It is recommended
                                                                                         Page 3 of 11


that the Save the Lampasas’ Brief be read in conjunction with this brief to save time by limiting

the need to switch between briefs.

       The Joint Applicants have identified Route 894 as the route best meeting the routing criteria

in Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 37.056 and 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC)

§ 25.101(b)(3)(B). Carpenter opposes this route and others that would have a devastating impact

on the Colorado River and its associated State Parks by crossing the Colorado just south of

Colorado Bend State Park and the Post Oak Ridge State Park. Carpenter also opposes Route 894

based on its devasting impacts to Greenwood Creek and the historic Carpenter Family property

aptly named Greenwood Creek Ranch. Although no crossing of the Colorado River is ideal,

Carpenter supports Joint Applicants’ proposed route 296 because it has reduced impacts to the

riparian areas in the study area by crossing the Colorado River in proximity to an area that is

already fragmented and traversed by pipeline corridors containing multiple pipelines.

       Carpenter does not oppose using the Links that comprise Route 894, or any of the other

Routes of interest, in Williamson and Bell Counties so long as the links do not then continue to

follow Route 894 in Burnet County. Instead, after Bell and Williamson counties, Carpenter urges

the ALJs and the Commission to follow the links in Route 296 or Route 572.


                                II.   ROUTING CRITERIA

       The point at which the proposed transmission line crosses the Colorado River is a pivotal

issue in this proceeding. A careful analysis of the record evidence demonstrates that Route 894,

which crosses the Colorado River on Link J22, is not a reasonable place to cross the Colorado

River. This analysis is contained in the Initial Brief of Save the Lampasas, and to avoid

duplication, is incorporated here by reference. Mr. Carpenter said it best:
                                                                                                  Page 4 of 11


                  The Colorado Bend region of Texas is widely known and cherished for its
                  unspoiled natural beauty, sweeping Hill Country vistas, serenity, abundant
                  wildlife, and exceptional recreational opportunities. Families, outdoor
                  enthusiasts, and visitors from across Texas are drawn to the area
                  specifically because it remains one of the few places where rugged
                  landscapes, dark skies, quiet solitude, scenic overlooks, rivers, waterfalls,
                  and native habitat have remained largely intact. The area surrounding
                  Colorado Bend State Park and the newly established Post Oak Ridge State
                  Park is particularly valued for hiking, camping, wildlife observation,
                  kayaking, fishing, swimming, photography, and enjoying scenic
                  overlooks that provide expansive views of an otherwise undisturbed
                  landscape. These scenic and recreational qualities are not incidental to the
                  area - they are the very reason people visit, recreate, and seek refuge in
                  the Colorado Bend region. It is an area that the State of Texas should want
                  to protect and preserve for all of its citizens to visit and enjoy. Introducing
                  a massive 765-kV transmission line across elevated ridgelines and
                  prominent viewpoints would fundamentally alter the visual character and
                  peaceful experience that makes this area unique and worthy of
                  preservation.1

        A.       Best Alternate Routes Under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

        Everything about Greenwood Creek Ranch is relevant to each of the statutory factors

related to routing in an intertwined way:

                      1.       Community Values

                      2.       Recreational and Park Areas

                      3.       Aesthetic and Historic Values

                      4.       Environmental Integrity2

        Route 894 would destroy and devastate the Carpenter Family’s Greenwood Creek Ranch

and all that makes it so special to visitors.3 Key aspects of Greenwood that would be permanently

devasted include:



        1
            Carpenter Ex. 1 Direct Testimony of John W. Carpenter at 13 (Carpenter Direct).
        2
            Tex. Util. Code 37.056(c).
        3
          Carpenter Ex. 1 (Carpenter Direct) at 23. The Carpenters’ Greenwood Creek Ranch is made up of Tracts
1635, 1637, 1640 and 1641 on the Applicants maps.
                                                                                          Page 5 of 11


                      1.   Colorado River Frontage;

                      2.   Views from the Main Lodge;

                      3.   Greenwood Creek and surrounding natural springs and pools; and

                      4.   The Mountain Top Lookout.

        Each of these impacts are contrary to preservation of community values, recreational and

park areas, aesthetics and historic values, and environmental integrity. The Carpenter Family has

preserved and protected the natural beauty of the Colorado River for almost 100 years to the benefit

of their community and nearby recreational and park areas, and unless derailed by the outcome of

this case, will continue to do so for generations to come. This portion of the Colorado River is

navigable, and the Carpenters have what appears to be the longest continuously occupied home on

its banks in the area.4

        The key features of Greenwood Creek Ranch that would be forever damaged by use of

Link J22 are depicted in this map from the evidence in this case.




        4
            Carpenter Ex. 1 (Carpenter Direct) at 23.
                                                                                                         Page 6 of 11




                                    Overview Map of Greenwood Creek Ranch5

         The impacts to the use and enjoyment of Greenwood Creek Ranch by using Link J22 would

be far reaching and irreparable.6 Greenwood has a rich and storied history and is a destination

location for hundreds of people each year who come to stay there.7 Greenwood Creek runs in an

east to west direction on the northern portion of Greenwood Creek Ranch. As such, Link J22 has

detrimental impacts to all aspects of the creek which would in turn have detrimental impacts on

the Colorado River.8 Unlike the other available links that cross the Colorado River, Link J22 has

a turning structure on Greenwood property within close proximity to the river.9 This turning

structure will have even deeper excavation and concrete footings than a new 765kV standard (or

tangent) structure.

             Id. at 9.
         6
             Id. at 6.
         7
             Id. at 7 and at Exhibit B History of Greenwood Creek Ranch.

           Carpenter Ex. 1 (Carpenter Direct) at 10; Carpenter Ex. 2 Direct Testimony of Crystal Hall at Exhibit B at
12 (Hall Direct).
         9
             Tr. at 32:5-23 (Cooley Cross) (Jun. 10, 2026).
                                                                                                    Page 7 of 11


        After that turning structure, the proposed link runs directly in between the guest cabin and

Greenwood Creek and is within the 500 foot notice corridor of that guest house.10 In addition, the

turn brings the line even closer to the Main Lodge, which was built by John Carpenter’s

grandfather,11 and parallels Greenwood Creek on the property as it runs into the Colorado River.12

        The environmental impacts of Route 894 to Greenwood Creek Ranch and its ecosystems

cannot be overstated. Corollary impacts on the Vann Ranch, with whom the Carpenters share a

fence line, and the images of Greenwood Creek and Simpson Creek that feed into it at the point

that would be crossed by Link J22 are documented in the testimony of Robby Vann.13

        On Greenwood, multiple streams and wetlands have been delineated that are likely to be

considered Waters of the US and therefore jurisdictional to the Army Corps of Engineers.14

Further, excavation required for the turning structure that would be required on Greenwood Creek

Ranch as well as other turning structures on Link J22 in vicinity of Greenwood Creek and Simpson

Creek could impact groundwater and would therefore require the approval of the Central Texas

Groundwater Conservation District (“CTGCD’).15

        Link J22 goes directly through (and by necessity over) the highest point on the property

which is the “Lookout” and would forever change the interrupted views from this vista.16 The

Lookout makes up the entirety of what the Applicants have marked as Tract 1637.17 It has been

part of Greenwood since the 1940s.18 Routing over this lookout peak will increase the already

atrocious visual impacts of the proposed line from both State Parks and from the remainder of

Greenwood and their neighbors.19 The full analysis of the record evidence with regard to why

Link J22 is inconsistent with the State’s commitment to the State Parks of Colorado Bend State

Park and Post Oak Falls State Park are reflected in the Initial Brief of Save the Lampasas and will

not be restated here.

                         5.   Prudent Avoidance

       There are multiple habitable structures on Greenwood Creek Ranch that would be severely

impacted if Route 894 were approved. Link J22 takes a sharp angle and splits between two

habitable structures on the property. First, is the guest house that is noted in the Application as a

habitable structure within 500 feet of the proposed Link J22.20 Link J22 is on the property where

the guest house is located.21 Second is the Main Lodge which serves as a gathering place all year

round for hundreds of guests, friends, and family. Although outside the 520 foot notice corridor,

it is less than 600 feet from the apparent centerline of Link J22, it is nonetheless a significant

source of exposure to the people that gather at Greenwood. 22 The 500 foot metric is simply a

notice corridor; it is not determinative of impacts to habitable structures or the people who use

them.23

                                                   III.    COST
          The cost to the consumers and the State of Texas cannot always be quantified and put in a

chart. The contingencies surrounding impacts to Waters of the US and endangered species impacts

associated with Link J22 are not separately quantified in the cost estimates in the charts. Further,

the intrinsic value in preserving and protecting the public investment in the 8,500 acres comprising

the Colorado Bend State Park and the Post Oak Ridge State Park and the associated viewsheds

which are integral to the public enjoyment of those parks cannot be entered into a chart.


                                  IV.     TEXAS PARKS AND WILDLIFE

          Before the Application was filed, Texas Parks and Wildlife (TPWD) sent a response to the

Applicants indicating the negative impacts of Links J22 and J24 (originally J2) to the Colorado

Bend State Park and the Post Oak Ridge State Park. In addition to noting the viewshed impacts of

this Link to both parks, TPWD offered this specific recommendation to avoid “ridgeline and

hilltops near TPWD properties of interest”.24 Especially by routing directly over the Greenwood

Lookout on J22, Route 894 is completely contrary to this recommendation. As acknowledged by

TPWD, “A 150 to 200-foot-tall transmission line and tower within 5 miles of a scenic viewpoint

valued for its natural qualities, is likely to be distracting to most visitors.”25




          23
               Carpenter Ex. 3 Direct Testimony of Barry T. Smitherman at 10 (Smitherman Direct).
          24
           Carpenter Ex. 1 (Carpenter Direct) at Exhibit F at 1; and Whiting Ex. 3 - Applicants’ Fifth Supplemental
Response to Glenn Hodge and Schwertner Farm, Inc.’s First Request for Information at 6.
          25
           Carpenter Ex. 1 (Carpenter Direct) at 14 (citing Application Ex. F, TPWD Input on Initial Proposed Link
J2 at A-893).
                                                                                                     Page 10 of 11


        Further, this same area of the Colorado River was put forward as a potential crossing by

LCRA in the past, and the Commission rejected that proposal as not being compliant with

applicable Commission criteria.26 In fact, Link J22 in this case is closer to Post Oak Ridge State

Park (a distance of 0.7 miles) than the proposed line was to Colorado Bend State Park, and still the

Commission found relevant that TPWD in that case found that the close proximity to Colorado

Bend State Park would compromise park use.27


                                               V.     PERMITS

        A.        Governmental Agency Involvement

        There are multiple permits potentially associated with Route 894 and the Applicants cannot

rule out the need for each of those permits. Each of these are discussed in the Initial Brief of Save

the Lampasas which is incorporated here. Specific to the Greenwood Creek Ranch, the evidence

shows that the consultation with the Army Corp of Engineers will involve impacts to the Waters

of the US and that a permit is likely to be required. This will at minimum add time and cost to the

completion of the project if Route 894 is selected.

        In addition, there are Golden Cheeked Warblers on Greenwood Creek Ranch which will

require consultation with US Fish and Wildlife Service.28 This complexity will also add to the time

and cost to complete the proposed project.




        26
             Id. at 14-15.
        27
           Id. at 15. See extensive discussion of this Commission precedent in the Save the Lampasas Initial Brief
incorporated here.
        28
             Id. at 19.
                                                                                         Page 11 of 11


                                      VI.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated in this Initial Brief, Carpenter requests that the ALJs recommend a

route using a Colorado River crossing on Link J31 and the Commission select Route 296.

Additionally, Carpenter respectfully requests any other relief to which it has shown itself entitled.

                                                 III.     COST

chart. The contingencies surrounding impacts to Waters ofthe US and endangered species impacts

associated with Link J22 are not separately quantified in the cost estimates in the charts. Further,

the intrinsic value in preserving and protecting the public investment in the 8,500 acres comprising

which are integral to the public enj oyment of those parks cannot be entered into a chart.

Bend State Park and the Post Oak Ridge State Park. In addition to noting the viewshed impacts of

this Link to both parks, TPWD offered this specific recommendation to avoid "ridgeline and

hilltops near TPWD properties of interest".24 Especially by routing directly over the Greenwood

Lookout on J22, Route 894 is completely contrary to this recommendation. As acknowledged by

TPWD, "A 150 to 200-foot-tall transmission line and tower within 5 miles of a scenic viewpoint

valued for its natural qualities, is likely to be distracting to most visitors."25
